content: Toprol-XL has been demonstrated to delay the progression of left ventricular end-systolic and end-diastolic volume increases after six months of treatment. In adults, metoprolol is rapidly and completely absorbed. However, following oral administration of conventional metoprolol tablets, plasma levels are approximately 50% of those achieved with intravenous administration, indicating about 50% first-pass metabolism. Metoprolol crosses the blood-brain barrier and has been detected in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) at concentrations approximately 78% of simultaneous plasma concentrations. Plasma levels after oral administration are highly variable. Only a small fraction of the drug (approximately 12%) binds to human serum albumin. Metoprolol is a racemic mixture of Rand S-enantiomers and is primarily metabolized by the enzyme CYP2D6. When administered orally, it undergoes stereoselective metabolism dependent on oxidation phenotype. Elimination occurs mainly through biotransformation in the liver, with a plasma half-life ranging from approximately 3 to 7 hours. Less than 5% of an oral dose is excreted unchanged in the urine, with the remainder excreted by the kidneys as metabolites that lack beta-blocking activity. Following intravenous administration, approximately 10% of the drug is recovered unchanged in the urine. The systemic availability and half-life of metoprolol in patients with renal failure do not differ significantly from those in individuals with normal renal function. Therefore, dosage adjustments of metoprolol succinate are generally not required in patients with chronic renal failure. Metoprolol is predominantly metabolized by CYP2D6, an enzyme absent in approximately 8% of Caucasians (poor metabolizers) and about 2% of most other populations. CYP2D6 can be inhibited by various drugs. Poor metabolizers and extensive metabolizers who concurrently use CYP2D6-inhibiting drugs will experience significantly increased metoprolol blood levels, which may reduce the drug's cardioselectivity. Compared to conventional metoprolol, plasma levels of metoprolol following Toprol-XL administration exhibit lower peaks, a longer time to peak, and significantly reduced peak-to-trough variation. Peak plasma levels after once-daily administration of Toprol-XL are, on average, one-fourth to one-half of those achieved with an equivalent dose of conventional metoprolol administered once daily or in divided doses. At steady state, the average bioavailability of metoprolol following Toprol-XL administration (50 to 400 mg once daily) is 77% relative to corresponding single or divided doses of conventional metoprolol. However, over a 24-hour dosing interval, beta-1 blockade is comparable and dose-related. The bioavailability of metoprolol increases with dose in a dose-related, though not directly proportional, manner and is not significantly affected by food when Toprol-XL is administered. The pharmacokinetics of metoprolol in adults are consistent with previous findings. Factors such as age, gender, race, and ideal body weight do not significantly influence metoprolol pharmacokinetics. Apparent oral clearance (CL/F) of metoprolol increases linearly with body weight. The pharmacokinetics of metoprolol have not been studied in patients under six years of age. Long-term animal studies have been conducted to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of metoprolol tartrate. In two-year studies in rats at oral doses up to 800 mg/kg/day (41 times the daily dose of 200 mg for a 60-kg patient on a mg/m² basis), there was no increase in the incidence of spontaneously occurring benign or malignant neoplasms of any type. Drug-related histologic changes included a mild increase in focal accumulation of foamy macrophages in pulmonary alveoli and a slight increase in biliary hyperplasia. In a 21-month study in Swiss albino mice at oral doses up to 750 mg/kg/day (18 times the daily dose of 200 mg for a 60-kg patient on a mg/m² basis), benign lung tumors (small adenomas) were more frequent in female mice receiving the highest dose compared to untreated controls. However, there was no increase in malignant or total lung tumors, nor in the overall incidence of tumors or malignant tumors. A repeat 21-month study in CD-1 mice showed no statistically or biologically significant differences in tumor incidence between treated and control mice of either sex. All genotoxicity tests performed on metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate were negative. No evidence of impaired fertility due to metoprolol tartrate was observed in a study in rats at doses up to 22 times the daily dose of 200 mg for a 60-kg patient on a mg/m² basis. In five controlled studies in healthy subjects, the same daily doses of Toprol-XL and immediate-release metoprolol were compared in terms of the extent and duration of beta-1 blockade. Both formulations were administered in a dose range equivalent to 100-400 mg of immediate-release metoprolol per day. In these studies, Toprol-XL was administered once daily, while immediate-release metoprolol was administered one to four times daily. A sixth controlled study compared the beta-1 blocking effects of a 50 mg daily dose of the two formulations. In each study, beta-1 blockade was measured as the percent change from baseline in exercise heart rate during standardized submaximal exercise tolerance tests at steady state. Toprol-XL administered once daily and immediate-release metoprolol administered one to four times daily provided comparable total beta-1 blockade over 24 hours (area under the beta-1 blockade versus time curve) in the dose range of 100-400 mg.
